title: Steering System and Vehicle Dynamics
summary: The steering system for our Formula Student car, designed alongside the vehicle dynamics team so it stayed clear of the drivetrain.
description: I was on a Formula Student team, and I was personally responsible for designing the car's entire steering system.
## Working with Vehicle Dynamics

I worked inside the Vehicle Dynamics team, six of us in total. While the rest of the team was developing the drivetrain, my job was to make sure nothing in it collided or interfered with the steering system as I designed it.
That meant checking clearances between the two systems throughout the design, and I also helped with smaller parts of the drivetrain design itself.
## Tools
The design was done in SolidWorks and Fusion 360.

title: Rear Diffuser, Audi TT Mk1
summary: A new rear diffuser for my Audi TT, designed in Fusion 360 starting from a 3D scan of the car.
description: I wanted a new rear diffuser for my Audi TT, so I started by 3D scanning the car and designed the whole part in Fusion 360 around that scan.
## Iterating on the design
From there it was a matter of iteration: working out the right size for the diffuser and how many fins it should have. This model is the final design that came out of that process.

title: Window Vents
summary: A pair of window scoops that route cool outside air into a car that has no air conditioning, even with the window nearly closed.
description: My convertible has no air conditioning, and on a hot day, or when it is raining and the windows have to stay shut, the cabin just heats up. I designed these two 3D-printed air scoops, left and right, in Fusion 360 to fix that.
## How it works
Each scoop catches the fast, cooler air outside the car and channels it through a small gap at the top of the window, straight into the cabin and onto you.
It is held in place by the window itself: you wind the window up and it jams the scoop into the slot, and a small clip keeps it seated.
## Result
It works well. I have driven with them up to about 150 km/h without any problem, and for a car without AC it is the one solution that gives airflow with the window almost closed.

title: Parametric Peristaltic Pump
summary: A fully parametric peristaltic pump designed in Fusion 360 to meter a viscous fluid at exact rates for a geothermal water-jet drilling system.
description: While working at a company that builds geothermal heating solutions for homes, I was part of a team developing a water-jet drilling system. It needed to carry a specific viscous fluid down the hole in very precise quantities and at very precise rates.
## A parametric pump

The most practical way to get that control was a peristaltic pump, so I modelled one fully parametrically in Fusion 360. That made the design easy to retune: tube size, the volume displaced per stroke, the number of strokes per rotation and other values are all parameters I could change in one place.
## Result
This is the final pump design I arrived at, and it worked well. The photos show the printed pump, driven by a power drill.

title: Parametric Scotch Yoke
summary: A parametric scotch yoke mechanism in Fusion 360 that turns a motor's rotation into precisely timed back-and-forth motion for a glass artist's installation.
description: A friend of mine is an artist who works with glass. For one of her installations a bar had to move back and forth with very precise timing and an adjustable range of motion. I designed the mechanism for it.
## Why a scotch yoke
The job was to turn the rotation of a motor into linear back-and-forth motion, and a scotch yoke was the mechanism I chose for it.
## Parametric motion
I built it parametrically in Fusion 360, so the range of motion is adjustable, and so is the character of the movement: from a juddering, shuddering motion, to a staggered one, to a very smooth one.
## Testing
We tested a lot. To work out the right sizing before committing to bought parts, I 3D printed the linear rails myself, and we also ran durability tests on the mechanism.

title: Tameboy
summary: A smartphone Game Boy attachment, dubbed the Tameboy.
description: I wanted a simple attachment for my phone that would let me play emulator and retro games anywhere.
I bought a cheap Bluetooth controller from 8BitDo and modelled a custom housing for it in Fusion 360, one that slots my phone in perfectly.
## Tameboy V2

I later made newer versions, called Tameboy V2, which use the MagSafe ring on the back of the phone to attach magnetically. That is the direction the product is developing in, and the latest version is the one in the pictures.

title: Desk Drawer Organizer
summary: A personal organizer with a dedicated slot for each thing I own, sized to fit exactly in my drawer.
description: A simple personal project: an organizer made specifically for the things I own, with a dedicated slot for each one, sized to fit the drawer it lives in.

There are slots for my ruler, my calculator, my power bank, my ID and business cards, and a lot more. I modelled it in Fusion 360, and because it is built somewhat parametrically, the slots and overall size are easy to adjust.

title: Blob Lamp
summary: A ceiling light inspired by cell division, with lamp blobs splitting away from a central form.
description: The Blob Lamp is an aesthetic overhead light, designed in Fusion 360 as a ceiling light.
## Inspiration
It is inspired by cell division: several rounded forms splitting away from a central one, the way a cell divides.
## Status
This is the initial design. I have not printed it, installed it or tested it yet.

title: The Perfect Buckle v25
summary: A parametric buckle, now on version 25, built to replace the closure on a World War II Dutch Army messenger bag.
description: This is version 25 of what I call, in my opinion, the perfect buckle. It was made for one specific use.
## The bag

I bought a World War II Dutch Army backpack-style messenger bag with a very odd closing mechanism. It did come with straps, though, so I repurposed them by putting a buckle on each side, which gives the bag a proper buckle closure.
## Always improving

I modelled the buckle in Fusion 360 as a parametric file, so every dimension is easy to change. This is the latest version. I am still testing it every time I use the bag, and I update it as things break, get better or worse, or I think of new features to add.

title: Worst Case Scenario v21
summary: A 3D-printed TPU bumper case for my phone, now on its 21st version, with a kickstand and tripod mount.
description: Worst Case Scenario is the phone case I keep making for my own phone, and this is version 21. Like the buckle, it is a project that is never really finished: I keep testing it and making new versions.
## The case
It is a bumper case. The front and back stay fully exposed, and big bumpers around the sides keep the glass from touching the surface if the phone is dropped.
It is printed at home in flexible 95A TPU, and it went through many versions to get the fit and sizing I wanted.
## Extra features
Along the way I added a kickstand and a tripod mount with embedded hardware. This is the version I am currently on.

title: Pole Placement Tool
summary: A multicolour 3D-printed marker that shows exactly where each tent pole goes and which way its guy ropes run, used during site visits and 3D scans.
description: The pole placement tool is a simple 3D-printed tool I made for the building team and the salespeople at my current company. It is printed in multicolour filament so it is very easy to see.
## Why it exists

When a salesperson visits a site to give a quotation, they also make a 3D scan of it, and that scan is the data I use to design the tent for that location. During the visit, they place this tool at each spot where a pole is meant to go, so the scan captures precise coordinates for where the team and the client imagine the poles. I can then put the poles in exactly those spots in the scan data.
## Showing the ropes

The tool also shows the direction of the pole and where its ropes will run out. That way the salesperson and the client can see, on site, that a pole facing this way means guidelines going out in these directions, and how far.
## Part of the pipeline
It is reusable, and it is one small part of the digital 3D-scanning pipeline for making stretch tents in custom locations.

title: Digital Fabrication Pipeline
summary: From membrane simulation to cutting pattern, floor plan and cost estimate, fully parametric.
description: This is the pipeline I built to take a custom tensile structure from an empty site all the way to production drawings. It is fully parametric, and it keeps growing in both directions: on the sales side and on the production side.
## Starting from a 3D scan

Every project starts with a 3D scan of the environment, not a laser scan. The scan gives me a dimensionally accurate, ready-made virtual world of the site, and I place my own 3D model of the tent straight into it.
## Designing the tent
I then design the tent virtually in Grasshopper, using objects for the poles, the guy lines and everything else in the system, and work out the form of the membrane from there.
## From form to production

The membrane geometry comes out of the Kangaroo simulation and is fed into another Grasshopper script that uses OpenNest. It automatically converts the geometry into a cutting pattern of fabric strips, optimised for roll width, with seam allowances added, panels labelled and a floor build plan generated that is easy to follow on the shop floor.
The same script produces a cost estimate for the sales team, with a full BOM and all the costs involved in a custom project. All of it is automated and parametric.
## Standard series

The same system does more than single projects. It produces standard series maps, like the one in the first picture, and a standard set of rules and plans for the production team covering a whole series of tents from 3 m to 30 m in half-metre steps. Drawing all of those by hand would have been practically impossible. With a system of rules behind the fabrication of these tents, it becomes a pipeline that can keep growing.
## Complex projects, simple code

Early on my scripts were rough, because I was still working out which components were needed and which controls were essential. Over time they became cleaner, and I distilled complex logic into tight, lightweight components: dense clusters of functionality packaged as simple drag-and-drop modules that can be reused again and again.

title: Scan-to-Quote Tool
summary: A web app I vibecoded with Claude that lets the sales team draw a tent on a 3D scan and get a draft cutting pattern, with quantities and waste, plus a DXF of the agreed shape.
description: This is a web app I vibecoded with Claude. You load in a .glb file, the kind of output a 3D scan from Polycam on an iPhone gives you, and then draw out a basic cutting pattern on it. The app does the calculations for you.
## Extending the pipeline

It does not replace the existing scanning workflow. It adds to the digital pipeline I had already built, and it puts a lot of that capability in the hands of the sales team. They draw the custom tent outline, set pole positions and heights, and the app generates a draft cutting pattern with material quantities and waste factored in. That gives sales a solid cost basis before design even starts.
## Better information for me

It also gives me better information. What I receive is a DXF of the shape that sales drew and agreed on with the customer. Export that DXF and it instantly populates a Grasshopper file with the exact specs, ready to run.

title: Tensile Structure & Metal Frame Design
summary: FEA/FEM simulation and design of tensile structures and the metal frames that hold them.
description: ## Tensile structures

Tensile structures are flexible, lightweight structures that can be varied widely within a working set of parameters: material properties, anchor points, poles and membrane shape are the main controls. Rhino with the Grasshopper and Kangaroo plugins were the right tools, and let me build a workflow in which a designer can virtually design these structures in high detail with endless customisability.
## Metal frames

Tensile architecture usually combines metal structures and hard elements with membranes and flexible elements, which all have to work together. I learned to model, design and optimise those frames using IQ Cube and Karamba, directly and parametrically connected to Rhino and Grasshopper. That made it easy to iterate quickly and optimise for strength, weight and cost: beam and bracing patterns, materials and profile options could be tested to find the best solution for each use case.

title: Tools for the Production Team
summary: Custom 3D-printed jigs, templates and cutting tools I made for the production team, such as a tool that cuts exact-width strips of keder.
description: I made a whole set of physical tools for the production team at my current workplace. Production involves a lot of very specific, repetitive tasks, and a purpose-made tool saves labour and gives faster, cleaner and more repeatable results than doing them by hand. They include custom measuring jigs, templates and strip-cutting devices.
## Keder cutting tool

The tool shown above cuts a strip of an exact width out of a keder profile that starts out much wider. You feed the profile through the tool, and a razor blade inside does the cutting. Press the blade with a finger so there is enough load to engage it, then pull the other end of the profile through the mechanism.
As you keep pulling, the blade keeps cutting, and you get one long strip of exactly the width you want, every time. It is a black 3D-printed part, and it looks very much like the model.
## Many more
This is just one of many tools of its kind that I have made for the production team.

title: 3D Scanning with iPhones
summary: iPhone scans instead of expensive laser mapping, giving more detail and letting the company take on more complex projects.
description: Most of our design phase now happened in Rhino and Grasshopper, so it made sense to develop the pipeline in both directions, on the production side and on the proposal and sales side, to link the customer and the production floor better.
## Scanning the site

That began with 3D scanning sites using iPhones, with Polycam, instead of the far more expensive and complex Leica laser mapper. It gives a much more detailed overview of even highly specific environments, including natural boundaries, water and trees.

A scan of a site takes between 5 and 15 minutes, depending on its size. The longer you spend, the higher the quality of the result. The salespeople doing the scans also gain experience over time and give me better and better results.
## Designing in the scan
The scan goes into Rhino and Grasshopper, where the tent is designed directly in the real site, with the poles, anchor points and membrane shape all driven by parameters.
## Built on site
Because the scans capture so much more of the environment, we could take on significantly more complex projects. These are some of the finished structures on site.

title: Resonance
summary: My own music player, built because I was done with Spotify: desktop and Android, with generated mixes, a tempo/energy "Tune" view, my own visualisers and a DJ mode. Screenshots use a fictional demo library.
description: ## Why I built it

I was annoyed with Spotify and wanted to get off it. Building my own player means I keep the best features I want and add my own ones that are actually useful to me: my own kinds of visualiser, my own EQ, everything tailored to exactly what I need.
## A player for the music you already own

Point it at your folders and it reads tags and cover art. It never moves, renames or modifies your files. Scanning runs in the background with a progress bar, and rescans skip files whose size and modified time have not changed. It reads MP3, FLAC, M4A/AAC/ALAC, OGG, Opus, WAV, WMA and AIFF.
## Made for you

The home page greets you, then offers mixes generated from your own library, with nothing external involved: one per substantial artist, one per well-populated decade, and Rediscover, which collects tracks you own but have never played. Each mix is a real page you can inspect, seeded by the date so it holds still while you browse and re-rolls tomorrow.
## Library

Songs (sortable), Albums, Artists and Recently played, with search across title, artist, album and genre. Artists are indexed per track, so a compilation lists its performers instead of a "Various Artists" bucket, and collaborations tagged "A; B" are filed under both artists.
## Tune

Resequence your library by ear with three dials and no black box: tempo, energy and brightness, plus a surprise slider that decides how much randomness to mix into the ranking. Play the result, play it next, or add it to the queue.
## Now Playing, visualisers and DJ

Click the bottom bar for a focused full-window view: a large cover with its colour bled into the background, big transport controls and what is up next. A toggle brings up visualisers: a segmented spectrum analyser with falling peak caps, an oscilloscope and a mirrored spectrum.
The DJ view adds two decks with tempo sync, key lock and a crossfade, so one track can be mixed into the next by hand or with Auto mix over a set number of seconds.
## Everything else

Cross-fade from 0 to 12 seconds, shuffle and repeat, a live queue you can reorder, user playlists, media keys and the system media overlay on Windows. Queue, position, volume and window size all come back on relaunch, paused and never autoplaying.
## On Android

Resonance for Android runs the desktop interface in a WebView and does natively only what a phone has to: reading the music on the device, and playing it from a foreground service so playback carries on when the screen locks. Playback runs on ExoPlayer, and casting to Chromecast is supported.

The phone app shares the desktop renderer. Only the player and the bridge to the platform are replaced, so Home, mixes, albums, Now Playing and the visualisers behave the same way on both. A Connect mode talks to the desktop app over the network.
## Building and testing

A preview harness runs the web half at phone size with the native side faked, so the interface can be driven and the layout checked from a desktop. The checks cover local mode and Connect mode, and a static seam check catches the case where the desktop renderer imports something the Android overrides do not provide, which would otherwise leave the app unable to boot. I package it as an APK and debug it on a real phone over Android Debug Bridge.

title: TT MMI
summary: A Spotify display and remote for an old iPhone mounted in an Audi TT Mk1, with the real car spinning as a wireframe. Screenshots use the built-in mock mode.
description: ## A Spotify display and remote for the car

Built for an old iPhone XS mounted in an Audi TT Mk1: landscape, black and Audi red, with the real car spinning as a wireframe. It shows what is playing and sends transport commands. Audio keeps playing from the Spotify app; this reads the player state and controls it, and Spotify Premium is needed for the controls.
## The wireframe car

The wireframe is a real Audi TT Mk1 (8N) model reduced offline to its feature edges: 4,500 edges in 49 KB, drawn on a 2D canvas with no three.js and no WebGL. Keeping only creases and open boundaries keeps panel gaps, wheel arches and glass outlines readable, and depth-banded line brightness fakes solidity. Drag to spin it; let go and it drifts back to a slow showroom rotation.
## Library, queue and an honest visualiser

Tabs for Now, Library (playlists and recents) and Queue, a device picker and a settings sheet. Spotify does not expose the audio stream to the browser, so the visualiser can run in a synthetic mode that makes no claim to follow the audio, or use the microphone for genuinely reactive bars. The volume slider greys out and says why when the active device does not allow volume changes.
## No build step

Static files only: no framework and no CDN. Sign-in uses Spotify's PKCE flow, so no client secret is ever needed, and it installs to the home screen as a full-screen app. A ?mock=1 flag swaps in a fake Spotify backend for working on the interface without a phone or an account.

title: Pi-hole Launcher
summary: A one-button Windows control panel for running Pi-hole in Docker. Screenshots use simulated data.
description: ## A control panel for Pi-hole, no terminal

A Windows app that runs Pi-hole in Docker behind one big Start button. It is a control layer around Docker: it never bundles or reimplements Pi-hole, it orchestrates the official pihole/pihole container and puts a native-feeling interface on top.
## First run: prerequisites

On launch the app checks that Docker Desktop is installed and running, that Linux containers are enabled and that it has administrator rights. If something is missing it shows a guided fix-it screen with a one-click Docker download link and a Relaunch as Administrator button, instead of crashing.
## Onboarding wizard

A short wizard explains what is about to happen, then asks for the network adapter Pi-hole should attach to (pre-selected to the active connection, with a warning for wireless adapters) and a static IP on that subnet. The app suggests an address and pings candidates so it does not offer one that is already taken, and it reports port conflicts on the PC.
## Dashboard and settings

The dashboard shows the container state with live stats (queries today, percent blocked, top blocked domain, active clients), restart and stop, blocklist updates and a troubleshooting log console. Settings cover the upstream DNS provider, starting with Windows, changing the network, and removing Pi-hole, which asks whether to keep your blocklists.
## Engineering notes

Pi-hole runs on a macvlan network with its own LAN address, and two things fail silently in that setup, so the app guards against them. Wi-Fi adapters generally cannot carry macvlan traffic, so wireless adapters trigger a warning and the app pings the gateway from inside the container after every start. Docker Desktop always exposes its uplink as eth0, so the app always passes parent=eth0 and uses your chosen adapter only to detect the subnet and gateway.

Live stats are fetched with docker exec, which works even though the Windows host cannot reach a macvlan container directly. Docker is only ever driven through its command line with argument arrays, never shell strings.

title: Booklet Maker
summary: A local web app that turns an ebook into a print-at-home, fold-in-half booklet PDF. I made it to read one book on paper for under 12 euros instead of 40.
description: ## Why I made it

I wanted to read a specific book, and I don't like reading on a screen. The printed copy would have cost about 40 euros, so I bought the ebook instead, put it through this app and printed it at home on A4 paper. The whole book cost me less than 12 euros, and I ended up with this app out of it.
## From ebook to a printable fold-in-half booklet

Drop in an EPUB, PDF, DOCX, TXT, Markdown, MOBI or AZW3 file and get a PDF whose pages are already shuffled into sheets, so printing double-sided and folding in half reads correctly. It is a small local web app: everything runs on your machine and nothing is uploaded.
## Preview and partition
Every chapter or section is listed. Untick the parts you do not want in the printout (front matter, an index), drag to reorder, and click a section to preview its text.
## Typography and print settings

Paper size, font, size and line height, margins, page numbers (position and start number), justification, hyphenation and an ink-saving mode. Folding can be a single whole stack, or bundles of a few sheets (signatures) so thick books fold flat without the inner pages creeping out, and optional faint fold marks help with alignment.
## Two PDFs out

Generate produces the booklet PDF to print, with pages imposed two-up in fold order, and a plain reading PDF in normal order for proofing the text before using any paper. Layout is rendered with headless Chrome through puppeteer-core, and MOBI and AZW3 files are converted through Calibre first.

title: HU-3 Steering System
summary: Designing, engineering and manufacturing the steering system for a Formula Student race car during a six-month internship.
description: A much more technical project than anything I had done before. Most of the work was designing high-performance functional components, prototyping them, and testing them both physically and with SolidWorks simulations. It involved a lot of trial and error, and teaching myself race car engineering, which was fun.
## Designing in SolidWorks

The steering system was designed in SolidWorks, around the chassis and suspension of the car. The pictures show the render of the full car, a check of distances between the steering and suspension parts, the steering column and its joints modelled in the assembly, and a simulation run on one of the parts.
## Understanding the geometry

A big part of the job was learning how race car steering geometry works. At low speed the inside wheel has to turn with a smaller radius than the outside wheel, which is Ackermann steering, and the diagram shows the geometry that sets it.
## Prototyping and testing

Before anything was made in metal, I prototyped it with 3D printing, laser cutting, duct tape and zip ties. Laser-cut wooden plates and a printed part tested the fit, a full mock-up of the steering shaft with a steering wheel laid out the parts, and a mounted test piece showed how the column attaches to the car.
## Building it

After a lot of 3D printing, duct taping, cutting, SolidWorks, welding and even some maths, I finished the final parts list and sent the parts out for production. These pictures show welding, the universal joint on the steering column in the real car, a production drawing of one of the parts, and the chassis with the team around it.
## Running
Just a few months after my internship, the car was running and driving.

title: Moduwrap: Adjustable Snowboard Binding
summary: A snowboard binding whose flex can be changed after purchase: swappable stiffness members in the chassis and swappable trays in the highback.
description: ## Overview

This was my graduation internship project, carried out at the offices of Low Pressure Studios in Amsterdam under the supervision of the Bataleon, Rome and Lobster design teams. The outcome was a design report, a research report and three ready-to-ride prototypes printed in SLS.
## The problem

Bindings have become very adjustable for size, but almost nothing about their feel or performance can be changed once you have bought them. Each model targets one kind of rider, so a wrong choice, a better skill level or a different riding style can mean buying a new pair. The brief was to design a binding that is more adaptable in feel and performance without becoming complicated.
## The client

The project was done for Low Pressure Studios, the Amsterdam company behind Rome SDS, Bataleon and Lobster. The binding was designed for Bataleon, whose design language is modern and bold. I worked in a 15 to 20 week window, so research, ideation and prototyping had to run in parallel.
## Research and orientation

Snowboarding was new to me, so I started with the basics: the anatomy of a binding (highback, chassis, baseplate, base cushion, straps, ladders and buckles), strap-in versus speed-entry designs, and how the existing chassis types (Fullwrap, Asymwrap, unibody) change the feel. I watched grassroots reviewers, talked to the product manager and binding developer, and built a competition map of binding designs along four factors: silhouette, materials, texture and colour. That map shaped the look of the final product.
## Ideas and direction

After a whiteboard session and a session with the client, four themes were chosen to explore: adjustable flex (highback and chassis), a modular Moduwrap chassis, a conforming lattice base cushion, and pressure-distributing straps. Flex comes from the chassis (side-to-side, torsional and mid flex) and the highback, so those became the focus.
## The Moduwrap chassis

The idea: make one or both stress members of the chassis removable. With them in, forces reach the baseplate through four contact points, like a Fullwrap chassis. Remove one and it behaves like an Asymwrap with three. I built and tested four prototypes, mostly 3D printed in PLA and nylon.
Prototype 1: The first was too thin and the stress members did not fit.
Prototype 2: The second fitted the baseplate and let the stiffness members slide in and out.
Prototype 3: The third added a tool-free click-button lock, left and right markings and topology-optimised members.
Prototype 4: The fourth refined the click mechanism, the angle of the heel wrap and the surface transitions.

A simple rope-and-weight test (a constant 10 kg load) showed a clear difference in mid flex between the modes, roughly 10 mm of deflection. Heavier 60 to 70 kg tests checked structural integrity. It was not a lab-grade test, but it was the most trustworthy one possible in the time.
## The adjustable highback

I modelled more than 50 highbacks directly in CAD, placing each next to reference parts and moving on to the next, which sped up diverging and converging. They narrowed to three mechanisms: stiffness rods, replaceable keys, and swappable stiffness trays. The tray concept won. The highback itself is made from a soft TPU shell with an EVA foam core and is nearly a "no-back" feel on its own. Slide in a tray and the stiffness changes. The prototypes confirmed the body could be thin (about 4 to 6 mm), saving weight and cost, and tested a dovetail mechanism for tool-free tilt adjustment.
## The final concept

The final concept pairs the Moduwrap chassis in nylon with the soft highback and a set of trays in carbon fibre, bamboo, ABS and nylon. Soft, medium and stiff modes are chosen simply by which tray you slip in. Colour pops mark the parts a rider needs to notice. I chose a safe, modern-minimalist styling on purpose, because the time went into the mechanics.

The name Moduwrap comes from the modular chassis, which lets riders switch between two conventionally different riding experiences, Asymwrap and Fullwrap. Fullwrap sends your power straight to the board so the boot feels connected. Asymwrap moves more naturally with your legs and gives a smoother, surfier side-to-side feel. Moduwrap lets you switch between them for park, backcountry or powder, and suits riders who are progressing and want to try different styles.

The Flextech highback ships almost flexible enough to feel like no highback at all. The rider picks a tray in NylonGF, carbon fibre or weather-treated bamboo, giving three to five stiffness levels. Soft mode is forgiving and playful for freestyle and park. Medium balances response and flexibility for all-mountain riding. Stiff mode gives the support and stability for fast, aggressive carving, at the cost of needing more precise rider input.
## What I would do next

Riding tests come first, then testing materials and tray stiffness ranges, injection-moulding feasibility for the double-shot TPU and EVA highback, and optional aluminium braces in the chassis if rider feedback asks for them.

title: Lamps
summary: A collection of lamps I have designed, most of them 3D printed and some combined with other materials like aluminium extrusions.
description: I have designed a lot of lamps. Most of them are 3D printed, and some combine other materials too, such as aluminium extrusions.
## The ones shown here
Each model in the viewer is one of them. Use the arrows at the top of the 3D view to switch between Lampp, Lamp, Zeena and Lampshade.

title: Bag Webby
summary: An aesthetic handbag designed together with a friend, and 3D printed.
description: Bag Webby is an aesthetic design project: a friend and I designed a handbag together. The whole bag was 3D printed, and the model above is what it looks like.

title: Rope Holder
summary: A highly specific tool for pulling a rope without winding it around your hands.
description: This is a very specific tool, designed to pull a piece of rope in a particular way. It lets you keep a firm grip on the rope and slide along it while you pull, without the rope winding up or digging into your hands.

title: Standing Lamp Base
summary: A base I designed to turn a thrift-store ceiling light into a standing lamp.
description: I found a lamp at a thrift store. It was an overhead light with a tube light inside, and I wanted to turn it into a standing lamp. This is the base I designed for it.

title: Plug
summary: A plug for the top of a water jet drilling system that seals it as airtight as possible while still letting pipes pass through.
description: This is a plug I designed for the top of a water jet drilling system. It covers the top of the pipe and still has to let other pipes pass in and out, while keeping the connection as airtight as possible, so it has openings shaped for those pipes. To seal it, you hammer or mallet the whole plug into place.

title: Nothing Phone (2a) Community Edition
summary: A retro-tech design variant of the Nothing Phone (2a), made for a design contest: yellowed beige plastic with pops of orange.
description: ## The brief
For a design contest, I designed a new design variant of the Nothing Phone (2a).
## Retro tech
The idea was to be inspired by retro tech, which is why the phone has a yellowed, beige plastic colour with pops of orange.
## The model
The pictures show the 3D model I came up with: the beige and grey panels behind the transparent-style back, and a close-up of an orange button against the cream frame.

title: Water Jet Nozzles
summary: Nozzles for a water jet drilling system, prototyped in many geometries and printed with FDM, SLS and MJF.
description: ## Nozzles for water jet drilling
These nozzles were designed for the water jet drilling system I worked on at the geothermal heating company, the same project as the peristaltic pump.
## Many prototypes
Getting a nozzle to behave the way you want takes a lot of iteration. I made many prototypes in all sorts of geometries and printed them with FDM, SLS and MJF.
## What the models show

The first model, nozzles v2, is a segmented nozzle housing in a collar and mounting ring, shown with its loose parts laid out beside it. The second, nozzles, is the earlier set of nozzle heads lined up together, each a different geometry: ribbed and spiral-grooved bodies, domed heads, threaded bases and a hollow tube.

title: Bicycle Chain Guard
summary: A simple chain guard for my fixie, so my trousers stop getting caught in the chain.
description: A simple chain guard that I designed for my bike. It is a fixie, and my trousers kept getting stuck in the chain. This is the fifth or sixth version of the design, and the one that has worked best for me.

title: Metal Components for Mass Production
summary: Brackets, connectors and fittings, taken from design to production with manufacturers on three continents.
description: ## Iterating in Rhino and Grasshopper

Rhino and Grasshopper make it very easy to iterate on the geometry of these metal structures, and on the connecting elements that join them. I could walk through different section sizes of steel and other materials quickly, and see how each choice changed the design.

Besides the main tent work I designed many of the surrounding metal components: brackets, connectors, the parts that hold everything together. I worked through the full process: initial design, 3D printed prototypes, small-scale manufacturing runs to validate geometry, and then production relationships with manufacturers in China, India, Sri Lanka and various European countries, covering finishes, colour variants and material choices.

I worked with metal manufacturers in China, standard parts suppliers across Europe and textile manufacturers in India and Sri Lanka, and with manufacturers within Europe for prototyping and smaller runs.

title: Internal Digital Tools
summary: Sidewall calculator, DXF translator and other small tools shipped across departments.
description: From afternoon vibe-codes to weeks-long debugging marathons, I shipped internal tools across departments that turned messy, complex problems into clean, simple answers.

The sidewall calculator is an HTML tool for stretch tents: enter the wall dimensions and it works out exactly how many standard wall sections fit, with full offset and edge clearance accounted for, so sales staff no longer have to guess when quoting even the most complex projects.

The DXF translator takes any DXF file, pulls out all the text objects, translates them into the language you need and outputs a new DXF identical to the original, just in a different language. It helped the team collaborate with engineers in Czech.

title: Inflatable Tent Generator
summary: A modular Grasshopper script that designs an inflatable tent from just three parameters.
description: During my time at the company we moved into inflatables. What began as exploratory projects ended in a full-scale procurement contract. To support it, I built a modular Grasshopper script for modelling and designing inflatable tents.

These structures are all built around a core arch geometry, so the whole tent is controlled by three parameters: arch height, arch width and number of arches. From these the script unrolls the panels of each tube section individually, with all the marked positions for physical components such as welded fittings. It also handles splitting tubes into panels and the layout of components, deliberately offsetting elements so seams do not align, which reduces the risk of leaks.

title: PowerBase
summary: A desk charging station with two MagSafe pucks, two Qi chargers and a 120 W USB-C port, in transparent polycarbonate.
description: The PowerBase is a desk accessory that rethinks the charging station. Two MagSafe pucks charge two phones at once and let you dock a phone horizontally or vertically while it charges and idles on your desk. Two standard Qi chargers are embedded in the base. It also has two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, and one of the USB-C ports can deliver 120 W for fast charging of several devices.

The design is a transparent polycarbonate build, reminiscent of the aquarium iMacs of the past, so the visible wiring and electronics become part of the look. A physical 2-in-1 button on the front of the base works as a power switch and a time regulator: it lets you adjust the overall charging speed or power the device down entirely, which also helps prolong battery life.
## A prototype for home

Ideally the PowerBase would be made of slick polycarbonate with all the details, like the visible wiring, on show. To make a version for myself on my small FDM printer I had to modify the design: the scale was less dramatic, and so were the proportions. I played with the slicer to get a fuzzy surface texture that hides layer lines, and added creature comforts such as good cable management, a dab of wax to diffuse the indicator LEDs, and rubber feet. With that, the first prototype was done.

title: RS-71 EV Hypercar
summary: An EV hypercar designed with one goal: to be faster than any production EV in a straight line.
description: Inspired by the long-tailed prototype cars of years past, the RS 71 was designed with one goal in mind: to go faster than any production EV in a straight line. This is my vision of that vehicle.

At the core of the design philosophy was aerodynamic excellence. I sculpted the body to slice through the air like a blade, with a sinuous, sleek silhouette that minimises frontal area and reduces drag.

The canopy-style two-seater arrangement borrows from fighter jets: the passenger sits behind the driver, so both occupants get an unobstructed view of any opponent in a drag race, which streamlines the car even further.

A high-downforce track version was also envisioned, freeing up the underbody for venturi tunnels and adding a massive wing. The RS 71 was never designed to be mass-produced. Its exclusivity would make it the crown jewel of performance EVs and a halo product for the Mahindra brand: a limited production run, crafted with painstaking care in India, where each car would be a work of art coveted by enthusiasts and collectors alike.

title: Polestar Concept 99
summary: A concept hypercar for a Polestar brief: a new form of performance for the electric age.
description: The brief was to design a Polestar vehicle about the experience of performance and the advanced technical story that enables it in a sustainable way: a new form of performance, one for the electric age.

Concept 99 combines the insanity of the analogue supercars of the 20th century with the EV technology of the 21st, recreating that driving experience sustainably. Central to the design are a brutalist recycled-aluminium body contrasted with a streamlined cockpit. The three-seater layout gives the driver a faux single-seater experience and strong frontal visibility without compromising practicality, and a vertically stacked, mid-mounted battery pack gives the feel of a retro supercar (it will go sideways!).
## Track mode

Putting the car in track mode lowers the venturi tunnels underneath and makes the spoiler extra active. Regen at the front wheels is turned all the way up to emulate that liftoff oversteer, and 80% of the 1600 electric horses are sent to the rear wheels.

I envision the body made of recycled aluminium and the carbon fibre recycled from old race car components, which adds to the novelty and makes the car more sustainable. The greenhouse is coated in semi-transparent tinted solar cells that can trickle-charge the car when it is not in use.

title: BatBuggy
summary: A hyper-aggressive, Batmobile-inspired buggy: a modelling and rendering project.
description: This project focused on the modelling process and on post-processing in Blender and Photoshop. I concentrated on making stunning visuals rather than following a full design process, because the aim was to learn to make renders, both video and photo. The buggy itself is hyper-aggressive (it has rockets on the back!) and tries to hark back to the classic red and black colour scheme of Batman in the 60s.

"Throw caution to the wind" was the sentence thrown around a lot while designing it. I wanted to keep the forms basic but add enough detail and complexity for standout final images and videos. The buggy draws inspiration from the Batmobile of yore, combining fluid forms with strong boxy features to accentuate its utility, and I experimented with sharp, angular, bat-like features while keeping a rugged, utilitarian look.

And yes, it has underglow. I kept the colour scheme stealthy and black, with hints of red to draw parallels to the comic books. The entire design was done in Fusion 360, with rendering in Blender; the concept art combines Photoshop and Blender.
